title: Fast training of accurate physics-informed neural networks without gradient descent
claim: Splitting the problem into fixed random spatial features and time-dependent coefficients lets each loss term be solved separately by classical solvers.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; blue/orange color coding, network diagram with function plots
description: The figure has two framed panels. The left panel has an orange-to-blue gradient border and shows a small neural network. A 2-node input x connects through blue edges to a 4-node hidden layer labeled w_i, b_i, and orange edges connect that layer to a single output node û(x,t). A snowflake icon and the label 'sampled and frozen' mark the spatial basis functions. A blue plot of σ(w_i x + b_i) sits on the left and an orange plot of time-dependent coefficients c_i(t) sits on the right. A dashed line and arrows label '(1) Space-time separation'. An equation underneath, with braces labeled Space, Time and Frozen-PINN solution, sums the products of the two parts. The right panel has a black border. It breaks the total loss L = λ1 L_PDE + λ2 L_BC + λ3 L_IC into three boxes: classical ODE solvers, hard constraints, and a least-squares solve. A box labeled '(2) Decouple the PINN loss' closes the panel. Blue marks space and orange marks time throughout.
caption: Solving a time-dependent PDE with Frozen-PINNs via space–time separation: hidden layer parameters $w_i, b_i \in \mathbb{R}$ are sampled and frozen to define spatial bases \(\phi_i = \sigma(w_i x + b_i)\), where \(\sigma\) denotes $\tanh$ (left), while time-dependent output layer coefficients $c_i(t)$ are computed by solving an ODE (right). Colors match corresponding $\phi_i$ and $c_i$.
abstract: Solving time-dependent Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) is one of the most critical problems in computational science. While Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a promising framework for approximating PDE solutions, their accuracy and training speed are limited by two core barriers: gradient-descent-based iterative optimization over complex loss landscapes and non-causal treatment of time as an extra spatial dimension. We present Frozen-PINN, a novel PINN based on the principle of space-time separation that leverages random features instead of training with gradient descent, and incorporates temporal causality by construction. On eight PDE benchmarks, including challenges such as extreme advection speeds, shocks, and high dimensionality, Frozen-PINNs achieve superior training efficiency and accuracy over state-of-the-art PINNs, often by several orders of magnitude. Our work addresses longstanding training and accuracy bottlenecks of PINNs, delivering quickly trainable, highly accurate, and inherently causal PDE solvers, a combination that prior methods could not realize. Our approach challenges the reliance of PINNs on stochastic gradient-descent-based methods and specialized hardware, leading to a paradigm shift in PINN training and providing a challenging benchmark for the community.
